la:conj:enim.html:
ĕnim,
conj. [comp. of ĕ for pronom. stem i, and nam], a demonstrative corroborative particle. (Its position is regularly after the first word, or the first two or more closely connected words in the sentence; only in the comic writers sometimes at the beginning. Put after est in the fourth place: in eo est enim illud,: ab omnibus est enim, etc.,; al., see below. Put after quoque: id quoque enim traditur,; ; ; 27, 22; 30, 1; 33, 30; 36, 27; but not in Cicero, v. Madv. ad .—Sometimes it divides an apparent compound: quotus enim quisque,)
To corroborate a preceding assertion, like equidem, certe, vero; hence freq. connected with these particles, esp. with vero (v. under B.), truly, certainly, to be sure, indeed, in fact: Ch. Te uxor aiebat tua Me vocare. St. Ego enim vocari jussi, certainly, I did order you to be called, : ornanda est enim dignitas domo,: in his est enim aliqua obscuritas,in fact, indeed,: ille (Dumnorix) enim revocatus resistere ac se manu defendere coepit,in fact, indeed,: tum M. Metilius, id enim ferendum esse negat,it was really not to be endured,: enim istaec captio est,this is clearly a trick,: enim me nominat,positively he mentions my name,: enim non ibis nunc vicissim, nisi scio,you shall positively not go,; ; cf. : Th. Quid tute tecum? Tr. Nihil enim, nothing truly, ; so, nihil enim,; ; cf.: enim nihil,: Pa. Quid metuis? Se. Enim ne nosmet perdiderimus uspiam, : tua pol refert enim,: certe enim hic nescio quis loquitur,: certe enim,; ; .—So too in ironical or indignant discourse: tu enim repertu's Philocratem qui superes veriverbio!you indeed!: ex his duo sibi putant concedi: neque enim quisquam repugnat, Goer.; cf. ; ; ; ; ; ; : non assequimur. Isti enim videlicet Attici nostri quod volunt, assequuntur,; so (with videlicet),; : Ca. Faxo haut tantillum dederis verborum mihi. Me. Nempe enim tu, credo, me imprudentem obrepseris, yes, indeed, I believe you are trying to take me in, .—
Strengthened by vero, and combined with it into one word, ĕnimvēro (unlike enim, usually beginning the sentence), yes indeed, yes truly, of a truth, to be sure, certainly, indeed: enimvero Chremes nimis graviter cruciat adulescentulum,: enimvero, inquit Crassus, mirari satis non queo, etc.,; ; fin.: postridie mane ab eo postulo, ut, etc.: ille enimvero negat,and of a truth, he denies it,; so, ille enimvero,; : hic enimvero,: enimvero iste,.—In corroborating replies (cf. certe, I. A. 2.): Me. Ain vero? So. Aio enimvero, ; cf. : Sy. Eho, quaeso, an tu is es? Ch. Is enim vero sum, : Al. Tun' te abisse hodie hinc negas? Am. Nego enimvero, ; ; : Pa. Incommode hercle. Ch. Immo enimvero infeliciter, .—And in ironical or indignant discourse: Da. Ubi voles, arcesse. Si. Bene sane: id enimvero hic nunc abest,that, to be sure, is wanting here as yet,; : enimvero ferendum hoc quidem non est,; ; cf. ; ; ; 33, 46; 34, 58.
Transf.
To prove or show the grounds of a preceding assertion, for: haec sunt non nugae; non enim mortualia,: mihi vero omne tempus est ad meos libros vacuum: numquam enim sunt illi occupati,: quas (geometricas formas) ut vidisset, exclamavisse, ut bono essent animo, videre enim se hominum vestigia, et saep. —In parenthetical sentences: quocirca (dicendum est enim saepius), cum judicaveris, diligere oportet,; cf. ; : rumpor et invideo (quid enim non omnia narrem?), etc.,: di maris et caeli (quid enim nisi vota supersunt?), etc., et saep.—
Sometimes the assertion, the reason for which is given, is to be mentally supplied, ; cf. ; : Am. Qui istuc potis est fieri, quaeso, ut dicis, jam dudum, modo? Al. Quid enim censes? te ut deludam contra? etc., what then do you think? ; cf. ; ; ; —So the expression: quid enim dicam? commonly ellipt.: quid enim? qs. for what can be objected to the assertion just made? quid enim de T. Tatio Sabino dicam, : quid enim? fortemne possumus dicere eundem illum Torquatum?; ; ; Lucc. ap. ; ; et saep.—
To explain a preceding assertion, for instance, namely: Sy. Si futurum est, do tibi operam hanc. Mi. Quomodo? Ut enim, ubi mihi vapulandumst, tu corium sufferas, ; Sc Metuo maxime. Pa. Quid metuis? Sc. Enim ne nos nosmet perdiderimus, : Lu. Di me perdant, si bibi, Si bibere potui. Pa. Qui jam? Lu. Quia enim obsorbui, why because, ; ; ; ; : quod enim,: non igitur videtur nec frumentarius ille Rhodios nec hic aedium venditor celare emptores debuisse. Neque enim id est celare, quicquid reticeas; sed cum, etc.,: antiquissimam sententiam, tum omnium populorum et gentium consensu comprobatam sequor. Duo sunt enim divinandi genera, etc.,; cf. . See Hand, Turs. II. p. 374-409.

la:verb:enitor.html:
ē-nītor, -nīsus or -nixus (enixus, of bodily exertion, esp. of childbirth: enisus, of labor for an end, esp. of mental effort, etc.,
v.infra), 3, v. dep. n. and act.
Neutr.
To force or work one's way out; or (more freq.) to force one's way up, to mount up, climb, ascend.
Lit.: per angustias aditus et ingruentem multitudinem,; cf. ; : dum cohortes in aequum eniterentur,: adeo erat impedita vallis, ut in ascensu, nisi sublevati a suis, primi non facile eniterentur,; cf. ; ; : sol per ardua enisus,: in editiora,: in verticem montis,: enisae legiones in aperta,: Vitellius in editiora enisus,.—Poet.: viribus eniti quarum assuescant (vites),by whose strength they may mount up,: opibus fratris enisus,.—
Trop.: nihil tam alte natura constituit, quo virtus non posset eniti,.—
In gen., to exert one's self, to make an effort, to struggle, strive, sc. to accomplish something.—With ut: enitare, contendas, efficias, ut, etc.,; so ; ; ; : tantum celeritate navis enisus est, ut, etc.,: ab adulescentia ita se enisum ut ab optimo quoque probaretur,; et saep.—With ne: illud pugna et enitere, ne, etc.,; so fin.—Pass. impers.: ab eisdem summa ope enisum, ne tale decretum fieret,.—Less commonly with inf.: corrigere mihi gnatum porro enitere, Ruhnk.; so ; ; .—Absol.: ego, quod potero, enitar sedulo,; (twice); ; cf.: pro aliquo,: in aliqua re,: ad dicendum,: quod (acc. respect, v. A. and S. Gr. § 232, 3): quidem certe enitar,; cf. fin., Orell. N. cr.—
Act. (perh. not ante-Aug.).
To bring forth, bear children or young: plures enisa partus decessit,: enixa, with acc., prooem. § 4; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.—Absol., ; ; ; —
To climb up, ascend a place: Pyrenaeum et Alpes et immensa viarum spatia aegre,: aggerem,: totum spatium,.— Hence, ēnixus (ēnīsus), a, um, P. a.
Strenuous, earnest, zealous: faciebat enixo studio, ne, etc.,; cf. opera (with prompta), 2, 5, 30: virtus,: voluntas,: enixo studio petere,, ext. 1.—Comp.: opera,; .—*
ēnixa, that has ceased to bear, Schneid.—Adv.
ēnixe, strenuously, earnestly, zealously: expeto,: causam suscipere,; ; ; ; ; 26, 47: petere, et saep.—Comp., ; ; : enixius orare, Greg. M. Dial. 4, 38 al.: animum imperatoris enixius deprecari,; .—Sup., .—*
ēnixim, the same, Sisenn. ap. .!*? ēnixus or ēnīsus, a, um, in pass. signif.
Born: quod in luco Martis enixi sunt,.—
Impers.: ab eisdem illis regis fautoribus summa ope enisum, ne tale decretum fieret, striven to their utmost to prevent, etc., .

la:verb:eniteo.gloss: to shine forth or out, gleam; brighten
senses: to shine forth or out, gleam; brighten
la:verb:eniteo.html:
ē-nĭtĕo, tŭi, 2, v. n.,
to shine forth, shine out, gleam, brighten (class.).
Lit.: fruges enitent, Att. ap. ; cf.: myrtus floridis ramulis,: campus,: caelum,i. e. to become fine again, clear up,: tantum egregio decus enitet ore,.—
Trop., to shine forth, to be eminent, distinguished (a favorite expression of Cicero): quod in eis orationibus, quae Philippicae nominantur, enituerat Demosthenes,; cf. ; ; : virtus in

bello, ; cf. ; : oratio Crassi,; .

la:verb:enitere.gloss: second-person singular present active imperative/indicative of ēnītor
senses: second-person singular present active imperative/indicative of ēnītor

la:verb:enavigo.html:
ē-nāvĭgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
Neutr., to sail out, sail away.
Lit.: de ea civitate,: Rhodum,.—Absol., .—*
Trop.: tamquam e scrupulosis cotibus enavigavit oratio,has escaped from,.—
Act., to traverse by sailing, to sail over: undam,: sinum,: (Indum),.
la:verb:enavigo.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.

la:noun:enumeratio.html:
ē-nŭmĕrātĭo, ōnis, f.
enumero
,
a counting up, enumerating.
In gen.: malorum,: bonorum et malorum,: singulorum argumentorum,: oratorum,—
In rhetor. lang., a recapitulation (Gr. ἀνακεφαλαίωσις), ; ; ;

la:verb:enuntio.html:
ē-nuntĭo (enuncio), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to say out (esp. something that should be kept secret), to divulge, disclose, to report, tell.
Prop. (good prose): ut, quod meae concreditumst taciturnitati clam, ne enuntiarem, quoiquam,: sociorum consilia adversariis,; cf. : rem Helvetiis per indicium,; cf.: dolum Ciceroni per Fulviam,: mysteria,; ; cf. ; ; Caes, B. G. 1, 31, 2; 5, 58, 1 et saep.— With acc. and inf., .— Absol., —
Transf., in gen., to speak out, say, express, declare (for the most part only in Cic. and Quint. in the rhetor., dialect., and gram. signif.): cum inflexo commentatoque verbo res eadem enuntiatur ornatius,: sententias breviter,: obscena nudis nominibus,: voluntatem aliquam,; cf. ; : fundamentum dialecticae est, quicquid enuntietur (id autem appellant ἀξίωμα, quod est quasi effatum) aut verum esse, aut falsum, etc., —Cf. in the part. subst.: ēnuntiā-tum, i, n., a proposition, = enuntiatio, , and 12, 28.—
To pronounce, utter: (litterae) quae scribuntur aliter quam enuntiantur,; cf. ; ; : masculino genere cor, ut multa alia, enuntiavit Ennius, Caesell. ap. .

la:noun:en.gloss: The name of the letter N.
senses: The name of the letter N.
la:noun:en.html:
ēn, interj.
etym. dub.; cf. Gr. ἤν, ἠνί; acc. to Rib. Lat. Part. p. 34 sq. compounded of obsolete interjection e and enclitic ne, as in quin, etc.
,
lo! behold! see! see there! (class.; most freq. in Verg.; in Plaut. and Ter. often em, q. v.).
In presenting in a lively (or indignant) manner something important or unexpected (en habet vim indignationis, ).—With nom. (so usually, v. Krebs, Antibarb. p. 407): ubi rorarii estis? en sunt. Ubi sunt accensi? Ecce, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Müll.; cf. : en foederum interpretes,: en crimen, en causa, cur, etc.,: en Varus et legiones,: en Priamus, et saep.—With acc. (class.): en memoriam mortui sodalis,: en causam cur, etc.,: en habitum,: en animam et mentem,.—With pronouns: en ego vester Ascanius, 672; so, en ego,; : en hic,; ; ; cf.: consul en, inquit, hic est,: em illaec sunt aedes,: en cui,: en quod,.—With whole sentences: en mehercule in vobis resident mores pristini,; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.: en ecce,; ; , p. 243, 6.—Even en en occurs, .—
In interrogations.
To excite the attention of the hearer: en ibi tu quicquam nasci putas posse, aut coli natum?: en quid agis?; ext.— More freq.,
Manifesting the speaker's wonder, anger, or excitement.
With quid, cur, etc.: en quid ago?; cf.: en haec promissa fides est,; : en quid agam?why, what shall I do?: en quo discordia cives Produxit miseros?: en cur magister ejus possideat campi Leontini duo milia jugerum immunia?.—
With umquam (or in one word, enumquam): en umquam aspiciam te?ever indeed?; so very freq.: en umquam,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; : en erit umquam ille dies, etc.,; et saep.; cf.: enumquam ecquando, Paul. ex Müll.; and, enumquam, εἴ ποτε, καί ποτε, Gloss. Philox.: en usquam, οὐδαμόθεν, εἴπου, ib.—
With imperatives, to incite to action; Engl, Come! en me dato, : hos tibi dant calamos, en accipe, Musae,: en age segnes Rumpe moras,; so, en age dum,; ; ; .—Cf. Hand, Turs. II. p. 367-373.

la:noun:ensis.html:
ensis, is, m.
Sanscr. root as-, asyati, hurl; asi, sword
,
a sword, brand.
Prop. (almost exclusively in the poets; synon. with gladius, acc. to ; cf. also spatha, acinaces, sica, mucro, pugio),; Cic. poët. ap. ; and ; ; : ensem haesurum jugulo puto,; ; et saep.; .—
Meton.
War, ; ; cf.: lateque vagatur ensis, i. e. slaughter,.—
For defensor: MARCELLO ROMANORVM ENSI,.—
Royal sway, .—
Ensis, the constellation Orion, ; cf. ensifer.

one of the giants upon whom Jupiter hurled Ætna, ; ; ; ; ; ; Hyg. Fab. praef.

la:verb:enumero.html:
ē-nŭmĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to reckon up, count over, count out (class.).
In gen.: jamne enumerasti id, quod ad te rediturum putes?: dies, * : peculium,i. e. to rate, estimate,: pretium,to count out, to pay,. —
In partic., to enumerate in speaking, to recount, relate (so most freq.): enumerare possum, quae sit in figuris animantium descriptio partium,; cf. : stipendia,: proelia,: triumphos et domitas gentes,: vulnera, oves, (with narrare): plurima fando,: prolem meorum,: femineos coetus alicui,: Juniam familiam a stirpe ad hanc aetatem ordine,: ne de eodem plura enumerando defatigemus lectores,.

Entellus, i, m.,
a Sicilian hero, famous as a pugilist,

to swim across, sail across, etc.

ē-no, āvi, 1, v. n. and a.
Neutr., to swim out, swim away, escape by swimming.
Prop. (rare but class.): facile, * : e concha, * : in Erythraeam,; cf.: in terram,.—
Poet. transf., of flying, * ; * ; . —
Act., to traverse by swimming, i. e. to sail through a place (in post-Aug. poets): orbem fretis,: has valles,.

enarro
,

la:verb:enervo.gloss: to remove the nerves and sinews
senses: to remove the nerves and sinews
la:verb:enervo.html:
ē-nervo, āvi, ātum, 1 (scanned ĕnervans and ĕnervātum in ; contra ), v. a.
enervis
,
to take out the nerves or sinews.
Prop. (rare and post-class.): poplites securi,: cerebella,; : enervatus Melampus,i. e. unmanned,.—
Transf., in gen., to enervate, weaken, render effeminate (class.; esp. freq. in the part. perf.): non plane me enervavit senectus,: corpora animosque,: artus undis,: vires,: animos (citharae),: orationem compositione verborum,; cf.: corpus orationis,: incendium belli (with contundere),.—Hence, ēnervātus, a, um, P. a., unnerved, weakened, effeminate, weakly, unmanly: enervati atque exsangues,; cf. ; ; : philosophus (with mollis and languidus),— Transf. of inanimate subjects: ratio et oratio (with mollis),; cf.: muliebrisque sententia,: vita (with ignava),: felicitas,

la:verb:enucleo.gloss: to take out the kernel, stone, etc. from (a fruit, grape)
senses: to take out the kernel, stone, etc. from (a fruit, grape)
to make clear, explain, make plain
la:verb:enucleo.html:
ē-nūclĕo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to take out the kernels, to clear from the husk.
Lit.: bacas, Scribon. Comp. 233; ; : uva passa enucleata,.—
Trop., to lay open, make clear, explain (cf.: enodo, extrico, expedio, etc.): haec nunc enucleare non ita necesse est,; ; ; in lemm. —Hence, ēnūclĕātus, a, um, P. a.
Clear, pure, unadulterated: suffragia (opp. eblandita),i. e. given from pure conviction, free from impure motives,: reprehensiones voluntatum,pure, simple, (cf. shortly afterwards, voluntates nudas).—Plur. as subst.ēnūclĕā-ta, ōrum, n., the essence, the condensed meaning: ex diversis auctoribus enucleata collegi, 2.—
Of speech, plain, unadorned: genus dicendi,; fin.—Adv.: ēnū-clĕāte (acc. to B.), plainly, without ornament of speech, ; ; ; ; ; ; .—Comp., ; .— Sup., .

la:verb:enubilo.html:
ē-nūbĭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to free from clouds, to make clear (eccl. Lat.).
Lit., .—
Trop.: veritatem,

senses: to explain in detail, to expound
la:verb:enarro.html:
ē-narro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to explain in detail, to expound, interpret (rare but class.): omnem rem modo seni, Quo pacto haberet, enarramus ordine,; ; ; ; ; ; ; Spald.: poëmata, Spald.; ; ; .—Hence, ēnarrātĭus, adv. comp., more explicitly: scribere, (opp. breviter et subobscure); 13, 12, 5.

ē-nervis, e, adj.
nervus
,
nerveless, enervated, weak, effeminate (rare and postAug., for enervatus; cf. enervo): corpus, Petr. poët. 119, 25: homo,: compositio (with effeminata),; cf. orator (with solutus),: et fluxum spectaculum,; ; init. al.—Adv.: enervĭter, weakly: blandus, August. cont. Faust. 22, 50.

ē-nĭtesco, -nitŭi, 3,
v. inch. n., to shine forth, shine out, become bright (freq. in the post-Aug. per.).
Lit.: ut (oculi) in hilaritate enitescant,.—Poet.: enitescis pulchrior multo (Barine),.—
Trop., to shine forth, become distinguished: sibi novum bellum exoptabat, ubi virtus enitescere posset,: gloria,; cf. : facundia,; cf. : utque studiis honestis et eloquentiae gloria enitesceret,: plebs togā (i. e. pacis artibus),.

Prop. (good prose): ut, quod meae concreditumst taciturnitati clam, ne enuntiarem, quoiquam,: sociorum consilia adversariis,; cf. : rem Helvetiis per indicium,; cf.: dolum Ciceroni per Fulviam,: mysteria,; ; cf. ; ; Caes, B. G. 1, 31, 2; 5, 58, 1 et saep.— With acc. and inf., .— Absol., —
Transf., in gen., to speak out, say, express, declare (for the most part only in Cic. and Quint. in the rhetor., dialect., and gram. signif.): cum inflexo commentatoque verbo res eadem enuntiatur ornatius,: sententias breviter,: obscena nudis nominibus,: voluntatem aliquam,; cf. ; : fundamentum dialecticae est, quicquid enuntietur (id autem appellant ἀξίωμα, quod est quasi effatum) aut verum esse, aut falsum, etc., —Cf. in the part. subst.: ēnuntiā-tum, i, n., a proposition, = enuntiatio, , and 12, 28.—
To pronounce, utter: (litterae) quae scribuntur aliter quam enuntiantur,; cf. ; ; : masculino genere cor, ut multa alia, enuntiavit Ennius, Caesell. ap. .

Ennĭus, i, m.
Q. Ennius, the most celebrated Roman poet of the ante-class. period, the father of Roman epic poetry, born at Rudiae, in Calabria, 515, died 585 A. U. C.; ; ; .—Cf. respecting him, Teuffel's Gesch. der Röm. Lit. p. 157 sq., Bernhardy's Grundriss der Röm. Lit. pp. 188 sq., 360 sq., and the authorities cited by both.—
